content.thinking:
I'm planning the elephant's proportions and skeleton structure, sketching out the spine chain from hips through chest with realistic scale for an African bush elephant facing forward.

Working out the neck and head joint chain, extending from the chest tip through curved neck points up to the head position and orientation.

Now I'm sketching the body loft itself, defining cross-section stations from rump to chest tied to the hips and spine bones with varying widths and heights along the way.

Thinking about joint ownership along the spine path, hips and spine1 share a point so spine1 takes precedence, leaving hips effectively unused. I'll simplify by just assigning the spine bone to that segment and skip hips.

Next I'm defining the tail as a separate chain from hips with four points curving down and back, named tail1–tail4, with a tapering sweep radius and a tuft of thin spikes at the tip. Then I'm moving on to the legs, starting with the front leg shoulder joint placement.

Naming the three-joint chain per leg as shoulder/elbow/foot with an "L" or similar side suffix based on positive x being left, then sizing the leg tubes to taper from about 0.33 at the top to 0.26 near the ankle, and adding a flat toe-pad cylinder at the foot for ground contact.

I'm checking that the foot geometry doesn't sink below the ground plane — using a flat end cap instead of round on the leg sweep so it doesn't dip too far below y=0, and placing the toe pad cylinder so its bottom sits right at the floor. I'm also planning small pale toenail shapes spaced across the front of each foot.

Working out the nail embedding and foot joint positioning for the hooves, then moving to the hind leg geometry: root and target joints with knee bend direction, checking the bone lengths against the span distance to confirm a slight bend. Now I'm defining the sweep radius function for the front legs.

For the skin, I'm planning a procedural paint function on a gray-brown base that layers horizontal wrinkle creases using sine waves perturbed by noise, adds subtle countershading on the underside, and blends in muddy brown tones on the lower legs with a dusty reddish tint elsewhere.

Still writing skin shader...

Still writing color blending logic...

For the head, I'm thinking a simple scaled sphere geometry might work better than a full loft for the skull shape, rigged to the head joint with a bone-weighted path from the back of the skull forward.

Defining skull profile stations...

I'm adjusting the head height to sit slightly above the shoulder, raising the station y-values, and setting up the neck joint position connecting into the head sweep with a radius around 0.7.

Now I'm tapering the neck radius from the thicker body chest width down toward the head, checking that the sweep stations overlap cleanly with the body loft. Then I'm setting up the trunk chain starting at the front of the head, hanging down with a slight forward curve toward the ground.

Setting up 6 trunk joints with 5 spans, assigning it as a tentacle role parented to the head, and tapering the radius from 0.3 down to 0.075 with rounded tip caps. I'm also planning to paint wrinkle rings across the trunk surface using a sine pattern along its length.

Now I'm working out the trunk tip details, adding a darker nostril disc near the end of the cylinder based on the tangent direction of the final segment, positioning it slightly inset from the cap.

Adding the spike atop the trunk tip, then working on tusks: curving them from the mouth corners outward, downward, then forward and upward in a path of control points to mimic the natural African elephant tusk curve.

Checking that tusk width stays wide enough to clear the trunk radius at that height, nudging the tusk offsets outward slightly to avoid overlap, then setting up the sweep geometry with a tapered radius and ivory coloring, rounded at the base and pointed at the tip.

I'm shading the tusk with a gradient from ivory toward a darker tan near the tip to mimic staining, and considering adding a small pink gum ring at the base where it meets the trunk. For the lower jaw, I'm planning a separate joint positioned beneath the trunk base, angled slightly forward and down to support a small lower jaw piece.

Adding a small jaw frustum tucked mostly behind the trunk, then moving on to the ears — large, Africa-continent-shaped flaps extruded from an outline, hanging from the sides of the head and extending outward.

Defining ear outline coordinates...

The direction isn't critical for shading purposes, so I'll paint ears symmetrically using position and normal, making inner surfaces slightly pinker with thin dark purple vein networks via cell patterns. For the hinge, I'm adding a joint at the ear's attach point so it can flex rigidly on that bone.

Now I'm working out ear placement: adding a darker fringe at the lower tip and rim, then figuring out the attachment coordinates so the ear sits at the head's edge without colliding with the neck or shoulder region, accounting for outward lean as it extends.

Checking the ear's attachment point against the body outline, it looks like the leading edge reaches down to around y=1.55 near the shoulder, with the ear extending outward past the body's width so it clears the surface near the top. For the eyes, I'm placing them small and slightly sunk into the head's side surface, using the head loft to position them near the upper-front station.

Rather than guessing floating points, I'll use nearest-surface snapping to find the exact hit point on the skull mesh, then stick the eye geometry there robustly. I'm building the eye as a small dark sphere embedded slightly, plus an eyelid ring and a tiny white highlight sphere, and adding eyelashes as a ring of thin spikes around the upper half of the eye using angular placement from the eye part's orientation.

Now I'm considering extra skull details like a temporal gland streak below the eye and twin forehead domes, trying to work out the right head station coordinates for where these flattened spheres should sit on top of the skull.

Confirming the eye point lands near the skull side as intended, and that the loft-based surface placement works correctly before ears go on. I'm also considering whether to add subtle anatomical details like a spine ridge or scapula/hip bumps using squashed spheres for extra realism.

Skin paint handles continuity across sweeps and covers neck and shoulder wrinkles, so I can skip separate wrinkle geometry there. Checking the leg-to-body join, I notice the leg root radius makes it bulge slightly past the body's side width at the top, so I need to pull the leg x-position and radius in a bit to keep it flush like a real elephant's leg.

Working out front and hind leg spans, segment lengths, and bend directions now -- limbs should curve forward at the knee like elephant anatomy, with front and hind legs each getting one inner bend joint. Defining the leg radius taper...

Setting up the feet: pad cylinders with flat tops, slightly wider than the leg to create a swollen foot shape, with toenails placed around the front edge -- five on front feet, four on hind, spread in an arc.

Nails get a pale gray-tan color. Then I'm defining the tail as a tapering chain of segments shrinking from base to tip, with a bristly dark tuft ring near the end.

Still writing tuft code...

Now checking the tail path geometry: the chain has four points matching the four-point requirement for the spans plus tip. I'm noticing the rump's round cap at the loft end might extend beyond the path endpoint by its radius, potentially pushing the body further out than intended at z=-2.75 instead of -2.0.

Adjusting the end stations: using radius 0.75 caps on body sections pushes the rump boundary to around z=-2.45 and the front cap buries into the neck around z=2.3, which is fine since the neck is thick enough to hide it. Overall this gives a body length of roughly 4.8m from rump to front, plus the head extending forward, totaling about 6.2m front to rump including tail -- reasonably close to real body length proportions of 6-7m.

Now I'm working out the spine arch across stations so the back dips properly behind the shoulders like a real elephant: setting rump, hip, mid, shoulder, and neck y-positions and heights so the top profile rises toward the shoulder (around 3.45) and hips (around 3.35) while dipping slightly at mid-back, and adjusting the belly line so it sags lower at center to around 1.15 while keeping the top around 3.15.

I'm positioning anatomical details against the skull and head stations—placing the tusk bases just inside the head profile near z≈2.75-2.95, and anchoring the trunk base inside a head station so it emerges naturally from the front face of the head.

Realizing the rounded end caps extend beyond their stated path length (by their radius), which pushes the actual face front further out than intended—so I need to pull the last head station back to around z=2.75 and start the trunk path slightly inside that, around [0,2.35,2.9], tapering outward to the first trunk joint near z=3.25. The same cap overshoot applies at the rear of the head too, extending it back into the neck region.

Working through the head stations one by one now—adjusting positions, widths, and heights for S0 through S3, with the final cap rounding out around z=3.1. Then I'm laying out the trunk path points T0 through T5 with decreasing radii as it extends down and forward, figuring out where the tusks should anchor relative to the trunk's base width.

Now I'm placing the tusk curve points, making sure they emerge from the lower jaw area and curve forward and upward without colliding with the trunk, checking their tip position against the trunk's tip and settling on a tapering radius from about 0.1 down to near zero.

Checking overall proportions against real elephant anatomy, the tusk length and head/shoulder heights fall within realistic ranges. I'm also thinking about adding subtle surface details - mud on the lower legs, dust on the back, and a scatter of small dark bristle spikes along the head's dorsal ridge using a normal-based filter to place them naturally.

Adding bristle spikes to the forehead and back...

I'm also planning small anatomical details like a tear-stain streak below the eye, a temporal gland mark, visible ear veins, and leg creases near the knees to add realism without overcomplicating the part count.

Writing knee-cap bump placement code...

I'll skip genital and chest-hair detail but keep mud paint handles for the belly loft, and I'm checking whether the body-paint wrinkle noise, which uses horizontal y-banding on limbs, should also apply around the shoulder and neck region.

For body wrinkles I'm deciding horizontal bands work fine since elephant skin folds near the belly tend to run horizontal, then adding a second lattice of thin dark cracked-skin lines using a cell-distance difference to create polygon patterns layered on top.

Writing skin paint function...

I'm checking that the cell line width stays thin enough for the texel resolution, and dialing back the mud intensity since elephants aren't always caked in it—then double-checking the skin color palette values are reasonable.

Reconciling the low-poly aesthetic with painted texture detail, I decide to keep facets crisp by disabling smoothing on the sweep geometry for body, legs, and trunk, giving that faceted low-poly look while still allowing subtle paint shading.

Writing ear paint logic...

Now I'm working out eye details: dark amber iris sphere with a small white highlight offset along the normal, plus an eyelid ellipsoid. I'm placing eyes symmetrically on each side of the head by finding the nearest skin point and sticking the eye geometry there, then positioning the highlight sphere slightly offset outward along the frame's normal direction.

Then I'm adding darker eyelids over the eyes before placing the eyeball, and finally generating a ring of small lash spikes curving around the top of each eye using an angular range and tilt.

For the head, I need a surface hit test against the lofted sweep shape, and I'm defining the hips as the root spine joint with its own position and role, then setting up the chain parent relationship. I'm working out the limb function signature — passing root position, target, segment lengths, and bend direction arrays — and starting to define the leg chain for each side.

I'm settling on unique joint names for each limb: front legs use shoulder/elbow/foot naming, hind legs use hip/knee/foot naming, each suffixed by side. I'm also working out the parent joint for each leg root — front legs attach to the third spine joint near the chest, hind legs attach to the hips joint.

Now I'm sweeping the leg geometry along the chain with a varying radius array for a tapered limb shape, using skin-colored paint, six-sided cross-section, sharp (non-smooth) segments, and a round cap at the top transitioning to a flat cap at the foot so the foot pad connects cleanly. I'm sizing the foot pad as a slightly tapered cylinder so it sits flush against the leg's flat end.

For attaching the foot pad, I'm rigidly binding it to the leg's tip joint, falling back to the last joint in the chain if no explicit tip exists, positioned just above ground level so it sinks naturally into the mud. Then I'm defining the ear joints as hinges attached to the head, angled backward and outward based on side, setting up their direction vectors so the bone extends correctly along that diagonal.

Now I'm extruding the ear outline into 3D using the hinge joint's position and direction as the bone axis, with some thickness and bevel for a soft rounded edge, and checking that the outline's fourteen points form a simple non-self-intersecting loop as they trace clockwise from the base around the rounded tip and back.

I'm also considering whether to tilt the ear's thickness axis to flare outward slightly, but decide to keep the default orientation for simplicity. For embedding depth, I'm aligning the ear's leading edge against the head's surface at its half-width so the base sits flush against the skull.

Checking that the ear doesn't collide with the neck or shoulder, then skipping extra rim details like a fold ridge along the outline to keep things simple. I'm moving on to the jaw, using a frustum-shaped bone for the jaw and chin with skin coloring, and skipping any mouth tinting for now.

For the body, I'm setting up a sweep/loft along the spine chain to generate the torso surface.

Defining neck and head joints...

Writing trunk shading logic...

Working out the trunk tip geometry, I figure out the end point and tangent direction from the chain, then place two small nostril discs offset to either side along a perpendicular vector, oriented along the tangent.

Checking the math, the disc at 0.03 offset sits just slightly inside the tip sphere's surface and pokes out a touch, which looks right. Now I'm positioning a small finger/spike shape near the tip's upper side, basing it off the end point plus an upward and backward offset relative to the tangent direction.

Attaching this spike to the trunk's bone, then moving onto the tusk geometry — a swept shape with tapering radius, bone-attached to the head, with a round-to-point cap style and an ivory-to-stained-tip color gradient defined along the sweep path.

Adding the tusk gum base at the head's surface, checking the placement coordinates don't end up buried inside the head geometry.

Now I'm placing shoulder blade and hip bumps along the body surface using nearest-point lookups on the loft, then adding forehead domes and cheek bumps near the head top using similar surface-snapping logic with embedded sphere scales.

For facial detail I'm adding a dark elongated streak under the eye using a scaled stick sphere oriented vertically along the surface normal, then scattering small dark cones across the forehead as bristles, filtered to only appear on upward-facing surface points.

Skipping chin hairs and ear rotation for now, I'm tallying up the total part count across legs, ears, tusks, and bristle sticks to keep things manageable. For leg surface bumps, I'm finding the nearest surface point near each knee joint offset outward by the leg radius to place a small raised bump there.

I'm double-checking my imports to avoid unused-import type errors, confirming everything I've pulled in (THREE, builder, rng, catmull, limb, paint, noise, cells, mix, smoothstep, gradient) actually gets used, and dropping anything like frame or offset that doesn't. I'm also verifying the types line up correctly — paint functions returning proper color tuples, noise and cells taking position/size/seed, and stick options accepting a scale as either a number or vector.

Now I'm adding a meta export with name, description, style, and commit info, then working through the tail: attaching a tuft ring at the tail tip using its joint as a frame, with spikes angled outward along the tail's direction for a tapered look. I'm plotting the tail's path coordinates curving down and back, tapering the sweep radius from thicker at the base to thinner at the tip, ending in a small rounded cap.

I'm adding tail bristles (count 10) and checking the trunk joint placement against the head, then setting body sweep sides to 10 for a smoother loft. I'm verifying ground contact so nothing clips below the feet pads, confirming the surface-nearest-point hit function takes a plain array, and defining the jaw joint parented to the head with aim coordinates, followed by building the lower lip as a frustum box positioned just below the head's base.

Checking jaw box alignment against the head's bottom edge across segments, then moving to toenail placement — front paws get 5 nails spaced across a -56 to 56 degree arc, hind paws get 4 nails spaced -42 to 42 degrees, both sitting on the pad at a fixed radius and height. I'm now starting a generic leg-building helper that takes root and target points along with bend directions to construct each limb symmetrically for left and right sides.

Writing leg helper function...
